# Group

<span id="cluster"></span>

::: {.callout-note}
## Unreleased 0.3.3 API

This page describes `rf.Group` on `stage/0.3.3`. Configure its capacity with
`n_groups`; predictions and assignment records use `group`.

The default combines normalized identity likelihood, balanced initialization,
deterministic routing, and refinement using Group's own reconstruction
objective. Other fields can still train visible Group assignments through
ordinary backpropagation. Meaningful partition recovery, the correct group
count, and reliable reconstruction remain experimental; earlier downstream
reassignment proof scores do not establish this integrated recipe's quality.
:::

`Group` represents labels, such as merchants, using shared learned group slots
and a persistent vocabulary. Evaluate the resulting assignments against the
behavior your application needs.
[Category](category.qmd) is the simpler choice for independent label embeddings;
[Hash](hash.qmd) compares IDs without keeping a vocabulary.

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    amount=rf.Number,
    merchant=rf.Group(
        n_groups=64,
        mask=rf.Mask(rate=0.15, reconstruct=True),
    ),
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

One labeled payment:

```yaml
amount: 42.75
merchant: grocery
disputed: false
```

The reconstructing mask hides some merchant labels during training and asks
the model to recover them. Dispute supervision can train assignments for visible
merchants through their input embeddings. Reconstruction also trains the group
decoder and its adaptive balancing mechanism. Neither objective guarantees that
the groups match human categories.

A masked merchant must be identifiable from visible context to be reconstructed.
An unrelated payment amount cannot reveal an opaque merchant ID, and the hidden
dispute answer supplies no input cue. Repeated IDs and a downstream target alone
do not guarantee recovery of a meaningful partition.

## Input and options

Accepts scalar Boolean, integer, floating-point, string, or binary labels, with
one compatible Arrow family per field. Training grows the vocabulary;
validation, test, and prediction reuse it. Unknown labels remain `valued` and
use a shared unavailable assignment. Nulls have a separate state.

See [Online Vocabulary](../core-concepts/vocabulary.qmd) for automatic growth,
admission timing with workers/DDP, supported training strategies, and changes
during fine-tuning.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `n_groups` | required | Integer `K` fixes group width; `(lower, upper)` enables an adaptive balancing subset with `0 < lower <= upper`. |
| `p_unavailable` | `0.01` | Training probability of replacing known input labels with unavailable content. Reconstruction answers remain intact. |
| `ema_decay` | `0.99` | Smoothing for usage, assignment information, and range-adherence statistics, in `[0, 1]`. |
| `revive_temperature` | `10.0` | Nonnegative revival schedule control; zero disables inactive-group revival. |

An integer `n_groups=K` normalizes to `(K, K)`. The former `bounds` keyword
is rejected.

The upper bound fixes physical group width. A ranged `n_groups` allows callbacks to
revive unoccupied columns or merge similar active columns. Revival preserves
columns already assigned to a known identity, even when they are outside the
committed balancing subset. These operations do not guarantee equal use or
human-interpretable groups. Vocabulary growth expands label rows without
changing `n_groups`.

## Learning and inspection

The training process binds batch-local label dictionaries before forward.
Growth preserves existing IDs, learned assignment rows, exposure counters, and
supported optimizer state, including the shared unavailable assignment.
New identity rows cycle through available groups by index: one group starts
with assignment score `0.1`, and the others start at zero. The unavailable row
starts neutral. Vocabulary growth initializes new rows the same way.

Training and evaluation route an identity to its highest-scoring available
group. Training uses a straight-through softmax gradient to learn assignment
scores without drawing Gumbel noise. Repeated occurrences share a group while
the model state is unchanged.

A reconstructing mask is required to train the group head, refine memberships,
and update adaptive balancing. A plain visible Group can learn assignments and
content embeddings from other targets through ordinary backpropagation, but
creates no Group reconstruction objective and does not run refinement. See
[shared leaf options](../core-concepts/data-types.qmd#shared-leaf-options).

Reconstruction combines unweighted state classification with unweighted label
cross entropy through groups. Each available group's learned identity scores
normalize across the populated vocabulary, giving a label distribution for
that group. Predicted group probabilities mix these distributions into the
final label probabilities. Training and prediction share this scoring rule.
Labels sharing a group can retain different learned frequency priors;
normalization does not force equal probabilities. Unallocated identity rows,
retired groups, and the unavailable input assignment are not output candidates.
The decoder uses ancestor memory but opts out of direct sibling query
conditioning.

Unknown target identities contribute neither label reconstruction nor
balancing updates. Usage EMA, committed-group selection, and adherence use
known reconstruction targets only. After each training batch, an extension
callback sums probability evidence and known-target counts across DDP ranks,
including ranks with no selected Group objective. The update weights observations
equally even when ranks have different target counts. Empty global batches leave
this state unchanged.

Adaptive selection measures variation between predictions: the entropy of their
mean distribution minus their mean individual entropy. Identical uncertain
predictions therefore provide no evidence for extra groups. Smoothed information
selects the size of the committed balancing subset, and usage selects its columns.
Uncommitted candidate columns can still route identities and receive gradients;
the committed count is not a count of all occupied groups.

Merging redirects affected identities to the surviving group and retires the
redundant column. Retired columns have zero probability in embedding, decoding,
and public assignment output until revival. Merge and revival clear obsolete
optimizer history for replaced slices while preserving unaffected history.
Both operations skip parameter replacement when an affected parameter is frozen.
An epoch with no known targets also skips them. Known-input augmentation does
not remove that target's supervision. The auxiliary `loss.group` encourages
balanced use of the committed subset; it does not calibrate label probabilities.

Metrics separate vocabulary coverage from reconstruction quality:

| Metric | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `targets.known`, `targets.unavailable` | Known and unknown selected valued target counts. |
| `coverage.content` | Known / all selected valued targets. |
| `accuracy.content`, `nll.content`, `loss.content` | Known-label accuracy and unweighted cross entropy over populated labels. |
| `accuracy.all` | Correct known predictions / all selected valued targets, counting unknown answers as incorrect. |

Training scores describe the latest batch; validation and test aggregate counts
and sums across batches and DDP ranks. With no known targets,
conditional reconstruction metrics are `NaN`; state supervision remains valid.
See
[pretraining evaluation](../guides/pretraining.qmd#evaluate-vocabulary-coverage).

For an application-supplied trained `model`:

```python
labels = rf.Group.vocabulary(model, rf.Address("merchant"))
assignments = rf.Group.assignments(model, rf.Address("merchant"))
status = rf.Group.status(model, rf.Address("merchant"))
```

`labels` is an index-ordered tuple. Each assignment contains a group ID and
probabilities across all configured columns, with zero probability on retired
columns. Status exposes `committed` balancing-column IDs, `retired` column IDs,
and `usage` EMA. These inspection calls read local model state under DDP;
the training callback synchronizes adaptive updates at every batch end.

An idle model also supports `rf.Group.assign(model, address, label, assignment)`
for persistent changes and `rf.Group.override(model, address, assignments)`
as a temporary context manager. An assignment is a group ID or a nonnegative
probability vector of upper-bound width summing to one. These imperative APIs
reject retired group IDs or nonzero probability on retired columns. They
grow per-label storage before writing when necessary, preserving earlier rows,
the unavailable assignment, and group width. They cannot run while the model
is active or vocabulary state is shared with workers. Overrides restore labels
and assignments on exit; any expanded allocation remains available. Saving or
rebuilding during an open override is rejected.

## Prediction

`group` contains the best group's integer `value` and `probability`;
`content` contains the best populated vocabulary label and its probability.
Label probabilities are normalized over populated labels, excluding unused
capacity and the unavailable row. Labels use `large_string`; an empty
vocabulary yields a null label and zero probability.

Group confidence and vocabulary-label confidence answer different questions.
Labels can retain different learned scores even when they share one group.
Neither estimates the probability that an input belongs to the known
vocabulary. Evaluate cold-input populations separately.

See the [prediction envelope](../guides/prediction-output.qmd) for shared
state probabilities, `inferred`, and repeated shapes.

The [reconstructing Group proof](../proofs/group/reconstructing-category-labels.html)
reports internal convergence for repeated identities. Its page distinguishes
that evidence from partition recovery and held-out prediction. The
[plain-input control](../proofs/group/plain-input-is-dormant.html) shows why
downstream supervision alone leaves the reconstruction-driven adaptive state
dormant; it does not show that visible identity assignments cannot learn.
The [regime recovery proof](../proofs/group/regime-recovery.html) tests the
stronger claim directly: assignment agreement with hidden generating groups
and prediction quality on independent observations, against a no-regime control.


## Refining memberships

Fitting automatically refines a Group that has its own reconstructing mask.
The objective is to predict that Group's known identities from context, measured
by identity negative log likelihood (NLL). Refinement reads no other field's
targets or losses and needs no additional extension API or dependency. Other
objectives can still shape the same Group through ordinary backpropagation.

First, refinement records Group's contextual group probabilities on training
observations. Holding these predictions fixed, it tests each identity's
membership while holding every other identity row fixed in the normalized
likelihood. It proposes the uniquely best-supported rows together, then reruns
Group on separate validation observations. The complete proposal is accepted
only if Group's actual validation identity NLL strictly improves. The validation
pass recomputes context predictions; it does not assume they stay fixed after
assignments change.

Refinement runs at the next fitting validation start after at least 200 optimizer
updates since its previous evaluation. Ordinary validation and checkpoint
selection then measure the accepted mapping. Standalone `validate`, `test`,
and prediction do not refine assignments; test observations never choose them.

Calibration retains canonical Arrow observations after data preprocessing:
at most 4,096 training rows / 64 MiB and 1,024 rows / 16 MiB from the first
validation loader across ranks. The byte limits can retain fewer rows.
Re-encoding neither reruns preprocessors nor admits new vocabulary labels.
Only selected, known, valued Group targets supply evidence. Each coordinate
counts separately, including multiple identities in one root row and repeated
or nested branches; the retained geometry determines their positions.

Missing validation, no own reconstruction objective, frozen or overridden
assignments, and absent known targets cause refinement to skip with a reason.
Unknown identities provide no membership evidence. Unobserved identity rows
and tied candidate minima keep their existing rows. An accepted proposal
preserves each replaced row's total log-mass and the unavailable row, clearing
stale optimizer history only for
overwritten rows. Rejection or failed evaluation restores the previous mapping.

## Historical reassignment proofs {#experimental-predictive-reassignment}

The earlier experimental proofs select memberships using downstream numeric
or categorical prediction errors. That is a different objective from the
integrated Group identity NLL. Their improvements are historical evidence for
those recorded methods, not learning results for the current default.

The [numeric proof](../proofs/group/predictive-regimes.html) tests crossing
response curves, unequal group sizes, and different hidden group counts. It
checks prediction error, partition agreement, and the exact number of occupied
groups separately. The [categorical proof](../proofs/group/predictive-labels.html)
asks whether the approach also learns context-dependent label rules. Both
include controls that remove the persistent identity signal.

The [cost comparison](../proofs/group/reassignment-cost.html) reports matched
wall time and additional forward work for the original proof-local method.
Its CPU timings do not establish the integrated recipe's cost, GPU performance,
or total FLOPs. These experiments concern new observations of known identities;
they do not establish how an unfamiliar identity should be grouped or solve
Group-label reconstruction. Prediction quality, partition agreement, and exact
group-count recovery remain separate checks.
